Documento(s) de cenário:
--- Project Scenario 2.pdf ---
Unified University Inventory System (UUIS)
So basically right now we've got no single way of tracking 
everything the university owns across the faculties — 
computers, furniture, software licenses, rooms, even who's 
sitting where — and it's all over the place depending on which 
department you ask. Each faculty kind of does its own thing 
with spreadsheets or whatever old system they inherited, and 
nobody at the university level can just look something up and 
trust the answer. We want to build one system that everybody 
logs into, students, staff, IT people, deans, whoever, and 
depending on who they are they can see and manage the stuff 
that's relevant to them, but it's all sitting in one place 
instead of scattered everywhere. 
 
The way I picture it, once someone logs in (and for the people 
with more access we probably want something extra like a voice 
check, not just a password) they land on a menu where they can 
look up people, assets, locations and licenses, add new ones, 
edit them, get rid of stuff that's no longer around. Nothing 
should ever really disappear though, more like get marked as 
inactive so we keep history. People should also be able to 
lump assets or rooms into groups, like all the printers on a 
floor, or split things into subgroups, and bring in old data 
from CSV files from whatever system they're using today 
instead of typing everything from scratch. 
 
There's also this whole request and approval thing that 
matters a lot to us. If someone wants to move an item, report 
something broken, or just ask for a new asset, they should be 
able to submit that and it goes up to whoever's one level 
above them to approve or deny it, and if they say no they need 
to actually explain why. The exception is the people at the 
very top, university-level admins basically, their requests 
just go through automatically since there's nobody above to 
check them. Speaking of levels, this is kind of the backbone 
of the whole thing: department, faculty, university, and then 
a base user level, and what you can see and touch depends on 
where you sit, a faculty admin can reach into all the 
departments under them but a department admin only sees their 
own patch. 
 
We also want decent search, both a quick one where you just 
type something and a more detailed one where you can filter by 
different fields and combine conditions, plus some basic 
reporting, like comparing how many chairs or computers a room 
has against its supposed capacity. And everything anyone does 
in the system needs to get logged somewhere so if there's ever 
a question about who changed what, someone with the right 
permission can pull that up. 
 
A couple more things that matter even if they're not the 
flashy part. We can't have more than about two hundred people 
hammering the system at the same time, so it needs to hold up 
under that kind of load without falling over. If nobody 
touches it for half an hour, just log them out automatically, 
we don't want sessions sitting open forever. And if something 
crashes or a connection drops halfway through someone entering 
data, whatever they hadn't saved yet needs to come back to 
them when they log back in instead of just vanishing, losing 
someone's work because the system hiccuped would be a 
nightmare. On the security side, everything going over the 
network needs to be encrypted properly, and let's put a 
CAPTCHA on anything automated so bots can't just hammer the 
login. 
 
Things like managing permissions themselves, creating new 
roles, tweaking what each role can do, that's more of an 
admin-only corner of the system and honestly not the part 
we're most excited about, it just needs to exist so the 
higher-ups can keep control. Multiple languages and that kind 
of polish, plus the heavier department and faculty specific 
functions, those can wait for a later version, we're fine if 
version one is English-only and covers the main stuff for now. 
What we really care about for this first round is getting 
people, assets, locations and licenses all visible and 
manageable in one web system that anyone in the university can 
log into through a browser without needing anything special 
installed.

Sistema: Unified University Inventory System (UUIS)

Resumo executivo: The Unified University Inventory System (UUIS) is a browser-based university-wide system for centralizing and managing people, assets, locations, software licenses, occupancy assignments, requests, approvals, searches, reports, and audit records. It replaces fragmented spreadsheets and legacy departmental systems with a single controlled source of inventory information, improving visibility, accountability, and administrative decision-making. 

Escopo: The UUIS must provide centralized browser-based management of university people, assets, locations, software licenses, requests, approvals, searches, reports, and audit records.
  Em escopo: User authentication and role-based access control
  Em escopo: Management of people, assets, locations, software licenses, and occupancy assignments
  Em escopo: Inactive status and historical preservation of records
  Em escopo: Asset and location grouping with subgroups
  Em escopo: CSV data import
  Em escopo: Requests for asset movement, failures, and new assets
  Em escopo: Hierarchical approval and denial workflows
  Em escopo: Quick and advanced search
  Em escopo: Room capacity comparison reports
  Em escopo: Audit logging and authorized audit consultation
  Em escopo: Browser-based access without special local installation
  Em escopo: English-language version 1
  Fora de escopo: Multiple-language support — explicitly deferred to a later version
  Fora de escopo: Advanced department-specific functions — explicitly deferred to a later version
  Fora de escopo: Advanced faculty-specific functions — explicitly deferred to a later version
  Fora de escopo: Advanced administrative permission customization — limited to the minimum capability required for higher-level administrators [INFERRED]
  Premissa: PA-01: University users will access the system through a modern web browser [INFERRED].
  Premissa: PA-02: Existing departmental data can be provided in CSV format.
  Premissa: PA-03: Organizational hierarchy data for departments, faculties, and the university will be available for configuration [INFERRED].
  Premissa: PA-04: Voice verification for privileged users will rely on an available voice-authentication capability [INFERRED].
  Restrição: REST-01 (Deployment): Version 1 must be accessible through a web browser without requiring special software installation.
  Restrição: REST-02 (Language): Version 1 must be English-only.
  Restrição: REST-03 (Capacity): The system must support approximately 200 concurrent users.
  Restrição: REST-04 (Scope): Advanced department- and faculty-specific functions are deferred to a later version.

Stakeholders:
  STK-01 - Student (Usuário primário): Access relevant people, assets, locations, licenses, and submit applicable requests.
  STK-02 - University staff member (Usuário primário): Consult inventory information and submit operational requests.
  STK-03 - IT staff member (Usuário primário): Manage assets, licenses, locations, assignments, imports, requests, and operational records.
  STK-04 - Department administrator (Usuário primário): Manage and consult information within the administrator's department and process subordinate requests.
  STK-05 - Faculty administrator or dean (Usuário primário): Consult and manage information across departments belonging to the faculty and approve subordinate requests.
  STK-06 - University-level administrator (Usuário primário): Manage university-wide information, roles, permissions, requests, audit records, and configuration.
  STK-07 - University management (Stakeholder externo): Obtain reliable university-wide inventory information for oversight and decision-making [INFERIDO].
  STK-08 - Legacy departmental data owners (Stakeholder externo): Provide historical inventory data in CSV format for migration.

Regras de negócio:
  RN-001 - Organizational access hierarchy: The organizational levels are base user, department, faculty, and university. Access scope is determined by the user's organizational level.
  RN-002 - Department visibility boundary: A department administrator may access information belonging to that administrator's department only.
  RN-003 - Faculty visibility boundary: A faculty administrator may access information belonging to all departments within that faculty.
  RN-004 - Historical preservation: Records that are no longer active must remain available for historical consultation and must not be physically removed from institutional records.
  RN-005 - Hierarchical request approval: A request must be submitted to the approver one organizational level above the requester.
  RN-006 - Mandatory denial justification: A denied request must include an explanation for the denial.
  RN-007 - Room capacity comparison: Room inventory reporting must compare the quantity of specified asset types assigned to a room with the room's stated capacity.
  RN-008 - Auditability: Every action performed in the system must be attributable to the acting user and retained for authorized consultation.

Requisitos funcionais:
  RF-001 - User authentication: The system must authenticate registered users using their credentials. [Must have]
  RF-002 - Privileged voice verification: The system must request an additional voice verification factor for privileged users [INFERRED]. [Should have]
  RF-003 - CAPTCHA protection: The system must require CAPTCHA validation for automated access attempts to the login function. [Must have]
  RF-004 - People management: The system must allow authorized users to create, view, update, and inactivate person records. [Must have]
  RF-005 - Asset management: The system must allow authorized users to create, view, update, and inactivate asset records. [Must have]
  RF-006 - Location management: The system must allow authorized users to create, view, update, and inactivate location records. [Must have]
  RF-007 - Software license management: The system must allow authorized users to create, view, update, and inactivate software license records. [Must have]
  RF-008 - Occupancy assignment: The system must allow authorized users to associate a person with a location or assigned position. [Must have]
  RF-009 - Grouping: The system must allow authorized users to create groups of assets or locations. [Should have]
  RF-010 - Subgrouping: The system must allow authorized users to create subgroups within asset or location groups. [Should have]
  RF-011 - CSV import: The system must import eligible people, asset, location, and license records from CSV files. [Must have]
  RF-012 - Asset movement request: The system must allow an authorized requester to submit an asset movement request. [Must have]
  RF-013 - Failure report request: The system must allow an authorized requester to submit an asset failure report. [Must have]
  RF-014 - New asset request: The system must allow an authorized requester to submit a new asset request. [Must have]
  RF-015 - Request approval: The system must allow the designated approver to approve a submitted request. [Must have]
  RF-016 - Request denial: The system must allow the designated approver to deny a submitted request with a mandatory explanation. [Must have]
  RF-017 - Automatic university approval: The system must automatically approve requests submitted by university-level administrators. [Must have]
  RF-018 - Role-based visibility: The system must restrict displayed records according to the authenticated user's organizational scope. [Must have]
  RF-019 - Quick search: The system must allow users to search people, assets, locations, and licenses using a general search term. [Must have]
  RF-020 - Advanced search: The system must allow users to search inventory records using multiple field filters combined by conditions. [Should have]
  RF-021 - Room capacity report: The system must generate a report comparing room capacity with quantities of selected asset types assigned to each room. [Should have]
  RF-022 - Audit log consultation: The system must allow authorized users to consult records of actions performed in the system. [Must have]
  RF-023 - Role management: The system must allow university-level administrators to create and modify roles and their permissions. [Should have]
  RF-024 - Unsaved data recovery: The system must restore unsaved user-entered data after a connection failure or system crash when the user logs in again. [Must have]

Glossário:
  UUIS: Unified University Inventory System, the centralized system specified in this document.
  Asset: A university-owned physical or logical item, such as a computer, printer, furniture item, or software license.
  Location: A university place or position where assets or people may be assigned.
  Inactive record: A record that is no longer operationally active but remains stored for historical consultation.
  Organizational scope: The set of university departments, faculties, or university-wide records a user is authorized to access.
  University-level administrator: An administrator whose organizational scope covers the entire university.
  Faculty administrator: An administrator whose scope covers a faculty and its subordinate departments.
  Department administrator: An administrator whose scope is limited to one department.
  Request: A submitted demand for asset movement, failure reporting, or acquisition of a new asset.
  Approver: The authorized person one organizational level above the requester who decides a request.
  Audit log: A chronological record of actions performed in the system, including actor, action, target, timestamp, and result.
  CAPTCHA: A challenge used to distinguish human interaction from automated access attempts.
  CSV: Comma-Separated Values file format used to import legacy inventory data.

Base: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 §9.6 · IEEE 830-1998 §3 · Sommerville (2016, cap. 4)
O Documento de Especificação de Requisitos de Software (SRS) é o contrato técnico que descreve o 
que o sistema deve fazer e sob quais condições de qualidade. Ele serve de referência para 
desenvolvedores, testadores, gerentes e clientes durante todo o ciclo de vida do projeto.
1.1 Artefatos Obrigatórios e sua Ordem
Um SRS completo e formal deve conter os seguintes artefatos, nesta ordem:
• ESCOPO: Define o que está DENTRO e FORA do projeto. Evita scope creep.
• STAKEHOLDERS: Lista todos os envolvidos: quem usa, quem financia, quem é afetado.
• PREMISSAS E RESTRIÇÕES: Fatos assumidos como verdadeiros e limites impostos ao projeto.
• REGRAS DE NEGÓCIO (RN): Políticas, fórmulas e condições de negócio que existem independentemente 
do software.
• REQUISITOS FUNCIONAIS (RF): O que o sistema DEVE FAZER — comportamentos, serviços, respostas a 
entradas.
• REQUISITOS NÃO FUNCIONAIS (RNF): Como o sistema deve SER — atributos de qualidade 
quantificáveis.
• HISTÓRIAS DE USUÁRIO (HU): Necessidades na perspectiva do usuário: Como [perfil], quero [ação], para
[benefício].
• CASOS DE USO (UC): Interações detalhadas ator-sistema com fluxo principal, alternativo e exceções.
• CRITÉRIOS DE ACEITE (CA): Condições testáveis em formato BDD (Dado/Quando/Então) que definem 
quando o requisito está concluído.
• GLOSSÁRIO: Termos do domínio com definição precisa para eliminar ambiguidades.
1.2 Como os Artefatos se Interconectam
Os artefatos formam uma cadeia de rastreabilidade. Cada RF deve ter origem em um STK 
(stakeholder) ou RN. Cada HU deve ter pelo menos um RF associado. Cada RF e HU devem ter pelo menos um CA. Esta rastreabilidade garante que nada seja implementado sem justificativa de 
negócio e que tudo que foi prometido seja testável.
Cadeia de rastreabilidade mínima:
STK → (RN →) RF → HU → CA

A ISO/IEC 25010:2023 define 9 características de qualidade do produto. Todo RNF deve ser 
classificado em uma dessas características. A seguir, cada característica com seus sub-atributos e

1. Functional Suitability (Adequação Funcional)
 Functional Completeness — o sistema oferece todas as funções necessárias.
 Functional Correctness — as funções produzem os resultados corretos.
 Functional Appropriateness — as funções facilitam a realização das tarefas.
EXEMPLO — RNF — 1. Functional Suitability
O sistema deve calcular o imposto sobre o valor do pedido aplicando corretamente a alíquota de ICMS 
vigente para o estado de destino, conforme tabela oficial CONFAZ, com variação máxima de R$ 0,01 em 
relação ao valor de referência da Receita Estadual.
2. Performance Efficiency (Eficiência de Desempenho)
 Time Behaviour — tempo de resposta e throughput.
 Resource Utilisation — uso de CPU, memória, rede.
 Capacity — limites máximos suportados.
EXEMPLO — RNF — 2. Performance Efficiency
O sistema deve processar no mínimo 200 pedidos por minuto sob carga de 1.000 usuários simultâneos, com 
tempo de resposta inferior a 2 segundos no percentil 95.
3. Compatibility (Compatibilidade)
 Co-existence — coexiste com outros sistemas sem degradação.
 Interoperability — troca dados com outros sistemas.
EXEMPLO — RNF — 3. Compatibility
A API do sistema deve expor endpoints REST/JSON compatíveis com o padrão OpenAPI 3.0, permitindo 
integração com o ERP legado via OAuth 2.0 sem modificações no ERP.4. Interaction Capability (Capacidade de Interação) — antes 'Usabilidade'
 Appropriateness Recognisability — usuário reconhece a adequação do sistema.
 Learnability — facilidade de aprendizado.
 Operability — facilidade de operação.
 User Error Protection — proteção contra erros do usuário.
 User Engagement — interface envolvente e motivadora.
 Inclusivity — acessível a pessoas com diferentes capacidades.
 User Assistance — suporte ao usuário.
 Self-Descriptiveness — interface autoexplicativa.
EXEMPLO — RNF — 4. Interaction Capability
Um usuário sem treinamento prévio deve ser capaz de registrar seu primeiro pedido completo em até 10 
minutos. A interface deve seguir as diretrizes WCAG 2.1 nível AA.
5. Reliability (Confiabilidade)
 Faultlessness — ausência de falhas em condições normais.
 Availability — proporção de tempo em que o sistema está operacional.
 Fault Tolerance — operação correta mesmo com falhas parciais.
 Recoverability — recuperação após falha.
EXEMPLO — RNF — 5. Reliability
O sistema deve ter disponibilidade mínima de 99,5% ao mês (máx. 3,6h de downtime não planejado). Em 
caso de falha crítica, o sistema deve restaurar a operação normal em até 4 horas (RTO = 4h).

know what they really need. In addition, the BAs might not be talking to the right people or asking 
the right questions.
The features that users present as their “wants” don’t necessarily equate to the functionality they 
need to perform their tasks with the new product. To gain a more accurate view of user needs, the 
business analyst must collect a wide range of user input, analyze and clarify it, and specify just what 
needs to be built to let users do their jobs. The BA has the lead responsibility for recording the new 
system’s necessary capabilities and properties and for communicating that information to other 
stakeholders. This is an iterative process that takes time. If you don’t invest the time to achieve this 
shared understanding—this common vision of the intended product—the certain outcomes are 
rework, missed deadlines, cost overruns, and customer dissatisfaction.
User classes
People often talk about “the user” for a software system as though all users belong to a monolithic 
group with similar characteristics and needs. In reality, most products of any size appeal to a diversity 
of users with different expectations and goals. Rather than thinking of “the user” in singular, spend 
some time identifying the multiple user classes and their roles and privileges for your product.
Classifying users
Chapter 2 described many of the types of stakeholders that a project might have. As shown in 
Figure 6-1, a user class is a subset of the product’s users, which is a subset of the product’s customers, 
which is a subset of its stakeholders. An individual can belong to multiple user classes. For example, 
an application’s administrator might also interact with it as an ordinary user at times. A product’s 
users might differ—among other ways—in the following respects, and you can group users into a 
number of distinct user classes based on these sorts of differences:
■ Their access privilege or security levels (such as ordinary user, guest user, administrator)
■ The tasks they perform during their business operations
■ The features they use
■ The frequency with which they use the product
■ Their application domain experience and computer systems expertise
■ The platforms they will be using (desktop PCs, laptop PCs, tablets, smartphones, specialized 
devices)CHAPTER 6 Finding the voice of the user 103
■ Their native language
■ Whether they will interact with the system directly or indirectly
FIGURE 6-1 A hierarchy of stakeholders, customers, users, and user classes.
It’s tempting to group users into classes based on their geographical location or the kind of 
company they work in. One company that creates software used in the banking industry initially 
considered distinguishing users based on whether they worked in a large commercial bank, a small 
commercial bank, a savings and loan institution, or a credit union. These distinctions really represent 
different market segments, though, not different user classes.
A better way to identify user classes is to think about the tasks that various users will perform with 
the system. All of those types of financial institutions will have tellers, employees who process loan 
applications, business bankers, and so forth. The individuals who perform such activities—whether 
they are job titles or simply roles—will have similar functional needs for the system across all of the 
financial institutions. Tellers all have to do more or less the same things, business bankers do more or 
less the same things, and so on. More logical user class names for a banking system therefore might 
include teller, loan officer, business banker, and branch manager. You might discover additional user 
classes by thinking of possible use cases, user stories, and process flows and who might perform them.

396 PART III Requirements for specific project classes
Prioritizing by using business objectives
Enhancement projects are undertaken to add new capabilities to an existing application. It’s easy 
to get caught up in the excitement and start adding unnecessary capabilities. To combat this risk 
of gold-plating, trace requirements back to business objectives to ensure that the new features are 
needed and to select the highest-impact features to implement first. You also might need to prioritize 
enhancement requests against the correction of defects that had been reported against the old 
system.
Also be wary of letting unnecessary new functionality slip into replacement projects. The main 
focus of replacement projects is to migrate existing functionality. However, customers might imagine 
that if you are developing a new system anyway, it is easy to add lots of new capabilities right away. 
Many replacement projects have collapsed because of the weight of uncontrolled scope growth. 
You’re usually better off building a stable first release and adding more features through subsequent 
enhancement projects, provided the first release allows users to do their jobs.
Replacement projects often originate when stakeholders want to add functionality to an existing 
system that is too inflexible to support the growth or has technology limitations. However, there needs 
to be a clear business objective to justify implementing an expensive new system (Devine 2008). Use 
the anticipated cost savings from a new system (such as through reduced maintenance of an old, 
clunky system) plus the value of the new desired functionality to justify a system replacement project.
Also look for existing functionality that doesn’t need to be retained in a replacement system. Don’t 
replicate the existing system’s shortcomings or miss an opportunity to update a system to suit new 
business needs and processes. For example, the BA might ask users, “Do you use <a particular menu 
option>?” If you consistently hear “I never do that,” then maybe it isn’t needed in the replacement 
system. Look for usage data that shows what screens, functions, or data entities are rarely accessed 
in the current system. Even the existing functionality has to map to current and anticipated business 
objectives to warrant re-implementing it in the new system.
Trap Don’t let stakeholders get away with saying “I have it today, so I need it in the new 
system” as a default method of justifying requirements.
Mind the gap
A gap analysis is a comparison of functionality between an existing system and a desired new system. 
A gap analysis can be expressed in different ways, including use cases, user stories, or features. When 
enhancing an existing system, perform a gap analysis to make sure you understand why it isn’t 
currently meeting your business objectives.
Gap analysis for a replacement project entails understanding existing functionality and discovering 
the desired new functionality (see Figure 21-1). Identify user requirements for the existing system that 
stakeholders want to have re-implemented in the new system. Also, elicit new user requirements that 
the existing system does not address. Consider any change requests that were never implemented CHAPTER 21 Enhancement and replacement projects 397
in the existing system. Prioritize the existing user requirements and the new ones together. Prioritize 
closing the gaps using business objectives as described in the previous section or the other 
prioritization techniques presented in Chapter 16, “First things first: Setting requirement priorities.”
FIGURE 21-1 When you are replacing an existing system, some requirements will be implemented unchanged, 
some will be modified, some will be discarded, and some new requirements might be added.
Maintaining performance levels
Existing systems set user expectations for performance and throughput. Stakeholders almost 
always have key performance indicators (KPIs) for existing processes that they will want to maintain 
in the new system.

3.5 Glossários (L2)
Em cada iniciativa da ER que envolve mais de uma pessoa, há o risco de falta de um 
entendimento comum da terminologia, ou seja, que algumas pessoas interpretem 
diferentemente os mesmos termos. Para mitigar este problema, o entendimento comum 
dos termos relevantes é registrado em um glossário.
Um glossário é uma coleção central de definições para: termos específicos do contexto, 
termos cotidianos com um significado especial no contexto dado, abreviaturas e acrônimos. 
Os sinônimos (termos diferentes que indicam a mesma coisa) devem ser marcados como 
tal. Os homônimos (usando o mesmo termo para coisas diferentes) devem ser evitados ou 
marcados como tal.
As seguintes regras aplicam-se aos glossários:
▪ Gerenciar o glossário de forma centralizada.
▪ Manter o glossário ao longo de todo o desenvolvimento do sistema.
▪ Definir uma pessoa ou um pequeno grupo responsável pelo glossário.
▪ Usar um estilo e uma estrutura uniformes para o glossário.
▪ Envolver os stakeholders buscando um acordo sobre a terminologia.
▪ Tornar o glossário acessível a todos os envolvidos.
▪ Tornar obrigatório o uso do glossário.
▪ Verificar se os produtos de trabalho respeitam o glossário.

2 BACKGROUND
This section briefly describes ISO 29148 emphasizing the suggested process items with which 
the axes of analysis are established and presents the relevant aspects of RE and the UC 
paradigm.
2.1 ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148
ISO 29148 is a systems and software engineering standard that specifies the required 
processes to determine the product requirements (including services) of systems and software 
throughout the life cycle (ISO/IEC/IEEE, 2018), (IEEE-CS, 2014). ISO 29148 is aligned with 
ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 standard for software life cycle processes and ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 
standard for system life cycle processes (IEEE-CS, 2014). ISO 29148, in its first edition (2011), 
replaced the IEEE 830-1998, IEEE 1233-1998 and IEEE 1362-1998 standards, also related to 
requirements engineering (IEEE SA, 2011), becoming the main standard in RE by providing a 
model adaptable to different organizations (Selvyanti & Bandung, 2017). In 2018, the second 
edition was published, due to the need to adopt a framework oriented towards a more detailed C2-4
technical approach (Ward et al., 2018), and in Boyarchuk et al. (2020) the importance of having 
a structured process in RE to build a good software product is highlighted.
ISO 29148 establishes (ISO/IEC/IEEE, 2018): (i) a set of 3 main processes that are iteratively 
and recursively applied in the system and software life cycle (see Fig. 1); (ii) a set of 2 related 
technical processes; (iii) each main process is composed of activities with established 
objectives to achieve a correct identification and good description of requirements; (iv) a set of 4 
types of documents for requirements specification at business, stakeholder, system and 
software levels; (v) the concept of operations and System operational concept; and, (vi) 
guidelines to manage the evolution of requirements.
2.2 User-Centered Software Requirements
The user-centered software development approach (UCD), was stablished as a response to 
existing software development schemes, which in practical terms can be noted, were focused 
on the technical aspect of the software and associated hardware (De Bellis & Haapala, 1995), 
(Norman & Draper, 1987). The UCD gained some relevance with the publication of ISO 
13407:1999 Human-centred Design Processes for Interactive Systems (Juárez-Ramírez, 2017)
and after that, when the stakeholders are included into ISO 9241-210:2010 Ergonomics of 
human-system interaction - Part 210: Human-centred Design for Interactive Systems (Vidal et 
al., 2012). Finally, the latest edition of the ISO 9241-210 standard is, recently, from 2019 (IEEE 
SA, 2011). In short, as pointed out by several authors (Juárez-Ramírez, 2017), (Forbrig, 2016), 
(Nieva et al., 2016), (Wanderley et al., 2014), and the ISO 13407 standard itself (ISO, 2019), 
RE should allow to reach an understanding of the needs, attitudes, motivations and behaviors of 
users that are the basis for achieving successful products and services, with a wide margin of 
end-user satisfaction.

stakeholders.descricao: Base user (students, staff) — logs in with a password, access restricted to what is relevant to them.
Department admin — sees and manages only their own department's data; approves requests from base users below them.
Faculty admin — sees and manages all departments under their faculty; login requires an extra verification step (voice check).
University-level admin — top of the hierarchy; their requests are approved automatically, since there is no approver above them; manages permissions and roles.

regras_de_negocio.descricao: Higher-access users (department, faculty, and university admins) require an extra verification step (voice check) at login, in addition to a password.
Deleted records are never physically removed — only marked as inactive, to preserve history.
Requests to move an item, report something broken, or request a new asset go to the approver exactly one level above the requester.
Rejected requests require an explanation from the approver.
Requests from university-level admins are automatically approved, since there is no approver above them.
A faculty admin can access all departments in their faculty; a department admin only sees their own department.
Permission and role management is an admin-only feature.

historias_de_usuario.descricao: As a base user (student/staff), I want to log in and see only what's relevant to me, so that I can manage my own view of the inventory without irrelevant data.
As a higher-access user, I want to complete an extra verification step (voice check) at login, so that my elevated access is protected beyond just a password.
As a user, I want to look up, add, and edit people, assets, locations, and licenses, so that the inventory stays up to date.
As a user, I want to submit a request to move an item, report something broken, or request a new asset, so that the right approver can review it.
As an approver, I want to approve or reject requests from users one level below me, explaining any rejection, so that the requester understands the decision.
As a department admin, I want to see and manage only my own department's data, so that I don't interfere with other departments.
As a faculty admin, I want to see and manage all departments in my faculty, so that I have full oversight of it.
As a user, I want to search using quick search or advanced/filtered search, so that I can find records efficiently.
As a user with reporting access, I want to compare a room's capacity against its actual chairs/computers, so that I can identify discrepancies.
As an admin, I want to manage permissions and roles, so that I can control what each role is allowed to access.

casos_de_uso.descricao: Submit and approve request — a user submits a request (move item/report broken/new asset), the system routes it to the approver one level above, who approves or rejects it with an explanation (or it is auto-approved if the requester is a university-level admin).
Search inventory — a user performs a quick or advanced/filtered search across people, assets, locations, and licenses.
Import legacy data — an admin imports historical inventory data from a CSV file.
Generate room capacity report — a user runs a report comparing a room's stated capacity against its actual chairs/computers.
Manage roles and permissions — an admin creates or edits roles and adjusts what each role can access.

criterios_de_aceite.descricao: Given a higher-access user attempting to log in, when they enter their password, then the system requires an additional voice verification before granting access.
Given a user submits a request, when it is sent, then the system routes it to the approver exactly one level above the requester.
Given a university-level admin submits a request, when it is sent, then the system approves it automatically, without requiring further approval.
Given 200 concurrent users accessing the system, when they perform normal operations, then the system remains responsive without failing.
Given a user session with no activity, when 30 minutes pass, then the system automatically ends the session.
